piezas.titulo: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
piezas.resumenOriginal: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.” His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve. “ AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.” Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says. “I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.” IEEE can play a role in shaping AI development Saran joined IEEE in March 2025. “After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.” He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work . “We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.” Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

piezas.titulo: School-Based Occupational Therapy in MTSS: A Call to Action.
piezas.resumenOriginal: School-based occupational therapy practitioners (SBOTPs) are called to move beyond reactive services for students with identified disabilities and contribute to preventive, inclusive supports for all learners. The Every Student Succeeds Act and the adoption of Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) create a timely opportunity for SBOTPs to expand their role as Specialized Instructional Support Personnel within school-wide systems. However, current implementation remains limited by conceptual confusion, inconsistent definitions of MTSS tiers, insufficient data collection and progress monitoring, and fragmented service delivery. These challenges restrict SBOTPs' ability to participate fully in school-wide prevention and intervention efforts and perpetuate a narrow view of occupational therapy (OT) as primarily a direct service linked to special education eligibility. This call to action argues for the development of a clearly defined, stakeholder-informed, and evidence-based model for OT practice within MTSS. It also offers recommendations for coordinated action across research, education, and practice to strengthen role clarity, professional preparation, and implementation support. Together, these efforts are essential to advancing inclusive, preventive, and educationally relevant OT services that support participation and success for all students.

piezas.titulo: Cognitive impairment profiles in patients with cerebrovascular diseases: a latent profile analysis
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundCognitive impairment is an increasingly recognized condition predominantly attributable to cerebrovascular diseases (CVDs). It substantially diminishes patients’ quality of life and imposes considerable burdens on caregivers and healthcare systems. However, how cognitive impairment manifest across multiple functional domains in individuals with CVDs remains poorly understood, often resulting in generalized care plans that fail to meet patients’ specific rehabilitation needs. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of cognitive impairment and their associated factors in patients with CVDs using latent profile analysis (LPA).MethodsThis cross-sectional study was conducted using convenience sampling in a tertiary hospital in southwestern China from November 2023 to September 2025. LPA was employed to identify distinct cognitive impairment profiles among patients with CVDs. Multinomial logistic regression was subsequently performed to examine factors associated with profile categories.ResultsThe final three-profile model classified 474 participants into three groups: a mild impairment group (82.5%), a moderate impairment group (11.4%), and a severe impairment group (6.1%). The three profiles reflected increasing severity of cognitive impairment among patients with CVDs. Compared with the mild impairment group, higher NIHSS scores (OR = 1.222, 95 %CI = 1.126–1.326, p < 0.001) were associated with higher odds of membership in the moderate impairment profile. Male gender and lower NIHSS scores were associated with lower odds of membership in the severe impairment profile (all p < 0.05).ConclusionIn this predominantly hemorrhagic and neurosurgical cohort, the retained three-profile model represented different levels of MMSE-based global cognitive severity among patients with CVDs. NIHSS score and gender showed exploratory associations with profile membership. The applicability of these findings to broader CVD populations requires further validation.

piezas.titulo: A non-randomized trial of the effects of transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation on cognitive performance and resting state connectivity
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundTranscutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) has shown promise for enhancing cognition and emotion regulation. To date, most human studies have focused on narrow learning paradigms that limit our understanding of how taVNS influences complex, integrative cognitive operations. Moreover, the underlying mechanisms of taVNS are still not well understood.ObjectiveBuilding on preclinical findings that vagus nerve stimulation enhances cognitive flexibility and memory in animal models, this study investigated whether acute taVNS can modulate executive function and neural connectivity in healthy adults.MethodsUsing a quasi-experimental design, forty healthy participants received either active or sham taVNS while completing executive function tasks and adaptive cognitive training (BrainHQ). High-density electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded during stimulation to assess cortical activity and functional connectivity across frequency bands.ResultsMultivariate analyses demonstrated significant effects of taVNS on cognitive function and EEG. Post-hoc group comparisons showed that compared to sham stimulation, active taVNS was associated with improved BrainHQ performance and decreased delta-band connectivity in left frontal, central, and parietal regions. Delta-band connectivity during active taVNS was positively associated with pre-to-post improvements in mood. No difference in executive function tasks was found between active and sham taVNS. Sensitivity analyses using adjusted models showed that these effects were sensitive to age, sex, and education.ConclusionBy evaluating multiple dimensions of executive function, these exploratory findings suggest that active taVNS may influence selected aspects of executive performance and frontal–parietal delta connectivity, potentially reflecting enhanced neural efficiency arising from the interaction between vagally mediated neuromodulation and continuously adaptive cognitive demands. However, these effects did not survive multiple-comparison correction and should therefore be interpreted cautiously and replicated in larger, prospectively powered studies.

piezas.titulo: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
piezas.resumenOriginal: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. piezas.titulo: Complex Event Processing (CEP) With Apache Flink: What It Is and When (Not) to Use It
piezas.resumenOriginal: https://dzone.com/articles/apache-flink-1 Most teams working with Apache Flink think about stream processing: filter events, aggregate values, enrich records, join streams. This covers the majority of real-time data problems. But there is a specific class of problems that stream processing handles poorly: detecting meaningful sequences of events across time. Did this specific chain of things happen, in this order, within this time window? Complex event processing (CEP) is the tool designed for exactly this, and it works fundamentally differently from stream processing. CEP is a built-in capability of Apache Flink, available as open source and deployable at scales the old proprietary platforms could never reach. Yet it remains underused and misunderstood. This article is a practical guide to what CEP is, when to use it, how Flink implements it, and where it fits in modern data architectures, including agentic AI , which is covered in depth in the companion article.

piezas.titulo: Neuronal avalanches in awake macaque V1 and V4
piezas.resumenOriginal: Neuronal avalanches are cascades of synchronised activity whose sizes follow power law. Analyses of avalanches shed light on cortical dynamics operating near a critical point. In awake monkeys, avalanches were found in motor and premotor cortex, where they are invariant to temporal binning, detection threshold and the number of electrodes employed. Whether awake primate early visual cortex, which receives strong structured afferent drive, shares these properties has not been tested. We analyzed a public 1,024-channel resting-state dataset from V1 and V4 of two macaques. In both animals avalanche sizes followed power laws over more than 10-fold range, the exponent scaled with bin width as alpha proportional to delta-t to the power beta (beta = -0.045 and -0.031), and the distributions ended at a cutoff proportional to the number of electrodes analysed. Raising the detection threshold from 1.5 to 4.5 standard deviations (SDs) removed over 99% of events but changed alpha by only 0.02-0.05 per SD, whereas randomly removing the same events destroyed the power law. Per-electrode shuffling abolished all heavy tails. Eye closure shifted alpha, beta and the branching ratio by less than predefined equivalence bounds, far below the reproducible differences between recording sites. Avalanche organisation therefore extends to awake early visual cortex.

piezas.titulo: Therapeutic Climbing in Pediatric Practice: Therapist Perspectives on Mechanisms, Delivery, and Contextual Factors - A Qualitative Study.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Therapeutic climbing is increasingly used in pediatric occupational therapy, yet implementation practices and reasons for non‑adoption remain underexplored. This qualitative study examined how Austrian pediatric occupational therapists position therapeutic climbing within occupation‑centered, movement‑based practice; how they deliver it in community contexts; perceived benefits and mechanisms; and barriers to adoption, including non‑user perspectives. Semi‑structured interviews were conducted with 24 state‑certified pediatric occupational therapy practitioners (12 climbing users, 12 non‑users) and analyzed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis. Therapists described therapeutic climbing as a structured, safety‑oriented, movement‑based occupational therapy intervention delivered in individual, dyadic, and small‑group formats, typically progressing from separation and everyday task preparation through warm‑up to graded climbing, with explicit readiness criteria for height and rope work under high supervision. Belaying was used as closely overseen responsibility training. Reported benefits co‑occurred across domains: motor coordination and praxis, sensory regulation, attention and other executive functions, self‑efficacy, social responsibility, and strong motivation linked to therapeutic climbing's sport‑like framing in real‑world settings. Therapists attributed these effects to belay‑based trust and responsibility, graded exposure to height, dense problem‑solving with immediate feedback, visible progress, and ecological delivery in public gyms. Adoption depended on accepting facility partners, intensive logistics and training, safety/liability governance, and uncovered venue costs. Non‑users largely endorsed therapeutic climbing's rationale but cited lack of personal climbing practice, limited gym access, training and safety demands, and unreimbursed fees. Overall, therapeutic climbing was viewed as a promising, participation‑oriented approach; principal constraints were systemic rather than conceptual. Rigorous comparative studies with clear fidelity and context reporting are needed to identify mechanisms and specify for whom and under what conditions therapeutic climbing adds value.

piezas.titulo: Harm Reduction-Oriented Occupational Therapy for Substance Use Disorders: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceIdentifying factors associated with sustained engagement in harm reduction-oriented occupational therapy may help inform more accessible interventions for individuals with substance use disorders (SUDs).ObjectiveTo examine participant characteristics associated with sustained engagement in the Real-Life Program (RLP), a harm reduction-oriented outpatient occupational therapy program for individuals with SUDs, and to explore changes in occupational and psychosocial outcomes among participants who continued the program.DesignRetrospective cohort study.SettingSingle-site outpatient occupational therapy program.ParticipantsFifty-five individuals with SUDs enrolled in the RLP. Participants were classified into continued (≥47% attendance) and noncontinued (<47%) groups based on the median participation rate.Outcomes and MeasuresCanadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale-Japanese version, Shitsu-Taikan-Sho Scale, and visual analog scales for craving intensity and perceived connectedness to others.ResultsPrior self-help group experience was significantly associated with continued participation. Older age showed a nonsignificant association. No other demographic or clinical characteristics differed significantly between groups. Among participants who continued the program, COPM Satisfaction improved significantly, whereas COPM Performance, self-esteem, alexisomia, craving intensity, and perceived connectedness did not.Conclusions and RelevancePrior self-help group experience was associated with sustained engagement in the RLP. Among participants who continued the program, satisfaction with daily occupations improved, although the clinical significance of this change remains uncertain. The RLP may provide a feasible harm reduction-oriented occupational therapy option for individuals with SUDs who have difficulty engaging in abstinence-based treatment programs.
